messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Emotional Stress: Situations that make me feel strong emotions, Smoking: I smoke, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Vignette:
Raymond is a 57-year-old man who works as a private tutor, single, and lives alone in a mid-sized American city. He came to the intake appointment wearing a heavy jacket despite the mild weather, and he chose the chair farthest from the door, angled so that he could see both the entrance and the window. He spoke carefully, often stopping mid-sentence, not because he had forgotten what he wanted to say, but because, as he put it, the words simply would not come — he knew exactly what had happened to him, and yet when he tried to reach for language, the sentences dissolved before they reached his mouth.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Raymond was sexually assaulted by an acquaintance, a man he had known casually through a community education program. The assault occurred in the man's apartment, a place Raymond had visited only once before and had no particular reason to distrust. At some point during the evening, the man physically restrained Raymond — held him down, controlled his movements — and assaulted him. What Raymond returns to most persistently is not only the act itself but the specific, suffocating quality of being unable to move, of having his body used against his own will, of being made to do and endure things he had not chosen. He described this to the therapist haltingly, with long pauses, his hands pressed flat against his thighs.

In the weeks that followed, Raymond found himself unable to account fully for what had happened. His memories of the assault are, paradoxically, both vivid and incomplete — certain details are etched with a clarity that feels almost physical, while other stretches of the evening feel absent, as though entire minutes were simply removed. He has come to believe that his own body failed him that night, that it did not do what it should have done, and this conviction has settled into something permanent: that his body is no longer a reliable instrument, that it might betray him again in ways he cannot anticipate or prevent.

Raymond's work as a tutor — which he conducts primarily in students' homes or in library meeting rooms — has become a terrain of daily negotiation. When he enters an unfamiliar home for a new student, he feels the danger of the space before he can assess it, and he has begun declining new clients whose homes he has not visited before. In every room he enters, he selects his seat with deliberate care, positioning himself near exits, with a clear view of whoever else is present. When he is working with a male student or when a male family member is present in the household, his attention fractures — he finds himself watching the man's hands, his posture, the distance between them, cataloguing small movements for evidence of threat. He has lost two regular students in recent months because he cancelled sessions without explanation, and a third family asked him not to return after he abruptly ended a session when an older brother came home unexpectedly.

Outside of work, Raymond has progressively narrowed his world. He does not go to places he has not been before. He smokes more than he used to, sometimes standing outside for long stretches in the cold, and he has recognised that the cigarettes appear at the moments when something emotional is pressing toward the surface. He avoids any situation he anticipates will produce strong feeling — he stopped attending his church, declined a friend's birthday gathering, and has not been to his sister's house since the assault. Physical contact with others — even a handshake, even a pat on the shoulder from a well-meaning colleague — produces a reaction he cannot fully describe, only that it is immediate and that he will do almost anything to prevent it from happening.

He had come to believe that he was simply managing, that this was the shape his life had taken now. What finally brought him to seek help was a conversation with his sister, who told him quietly that she felt she had lost him. He arrived at the intake session uncertain what he was hoping for, but most afraid, he said, that there was no longer a version of himself that could be trusted — by others, or by his own body.
